items.title: HTB: Nimbus
items.summary: Nimbus is a Linux box hosting a job scheduler website backed by an emulated AWS environment. I’ll abuse a server-side request forgery in the job submission form, bypassing a string block list with a decimal IP address to reach the instance metadata service and steal AWS credentials. Those credentials can send messages to an SQS queue, where a worker deserializes them with PyYAML, giving a shell in a container. From there, I’ll find the worker’s credentials and go around an IAM proxy to talk directly to the Floci emulator. I’ll create a CodeBuild project with a privileged container, using a bash exported function in an environment variable to keep the build container alive, and abuse the kernel’s modprobe path to escape to the host as root.

items.title: FBI Reveals How Hackers Use ARTEX AI Agents to Gain Privileged Access in Under Three Hours
items.summary: The FBI has warned that hackers are using ARTEX AI agents to automate network attacks, with some intrusions reaching privileged access in under three hours. Its November 13, 2026, FLASH alert describes how attackers combine stolen credentials, exposed applications, and cloud permissions to shorten the gap between discovery and compromise. ARTEX is an open-source security testing framework, not a malware family. Written in Go, it connects external large language models to agents that turn instructions into commands. Operators set objectives while agents scan targets, run tools, review results, and adjust failed steps with limited human input throughout an attack campaign. ARTEX Accelerates Enterprise Attacks As covered in Cybersecuritynews.com’s ARTEX enterprise attack analysis , the framework links familiar weaknesses rather than relying on a single new exploit. Agents can investigate cloud permissions, map Active Directory, and test access paths. Google observed individual automated bursts lasting two to 25 seconds, leaving defenders little time to assess connected events. The FBI lists attacks involving SQL injection, missing API authentication, exposed passwords, and abuse of trusted cloud connections. After entry, agents have added credentials to existing applications, deployed web shells, and attempted credential theft. Other activity included searching for Windows systems without endpoint protection and mapping over 110,000 directory objects. Microsoft previously linked ARTEX to Storm-0940, a China-state-aligned group targeting Microsoft 365 environments through compromised ConnectWise application credentials. Attackers attempted access to more than 2,250 tenants using permissions customers had already approved. That number measures targeting, not confirmed breaches, and successful sign-ins alone do not establish customer data theft. The FBI advisory brings these findings together, warning that ARTEX also targets overlooked supplier portals, sales tools, and mobile backends. Its under-three-hour figure describes some observed intrusions, not a fixed capability. Publicly exposed consoles exceeded 1,600 by early November, although exposed installations do not automatically prove malicious use by their operators. A separate WorkOS breach report shows the risk to internal business applications. WorkOS detected unauthorized access to a sales application containing customer contact details and conversation records, including Slack excerpts. Its CEO identified ARTEX involvement, while the company reported no evidence that production services or WorkOS application data were affected. Another Microsoft investigation documented ARTEX agents searching GitHub for exposed secrets. In one case, an agent progressed from repository searches to stealing Azure Key Vault data within five minutes. The activity illustrates how leaked application credentials can become cloud access, particularly when those identities hold broad permissions across connected services. Researchers also examined servers exposed by an operator linked to South Korean financial attacks. The files revealed AI routing tools, reusable instructions, proxy services, and stored credentials. Those attacks affected roughly 67,000 people. However, shared ARTEX use does not establish that this operator, Storm-0940, and the WorkOS attacker were connected. What Security Teams Should Monitor The FBI recommends restricting exposed administration tools, reducing application permissions, and scanning repositories for secrets. Defenders should connect unusual application sign-ins with credential additions, role changes, and rapid API activity. items.title: Microsoft Warns of Active Password Stealing Attack Exploiting the Microsoft 365 Service Disruption
items.summary: Microsoft has warned of an active phishing campaign using the November 12 Microsoft 365 service disruption to lure users into opening fake email recovery links. The messages copy Microsoft service health notices and cite the real Exchange Online incident EX1550543, making the requests appear linked to an ongoing business problem. Microsoft Threat Intelligence detected emails on November 13 claiming that messages held during the outage would be deleted within 24 hours unless recipients clicked to restore them. That deadline creates pressure to act quickly, particularly for employees already worried about missing customer messages, delayed payments, or other urgent business communications. The warning follows the Microsoft 365 outage that affected Exchange Online and other cloud services . The phishing campaign takes advantage of that disruption, but it should not be confused with its cause. Microsoft’s outage updates said there was no indication that malicious activity had caused the underlying service failure. Active Password Stealing Attack The phishing emails use subject lines following the pattern “Outage – [six-character code].” Sender display names include organization-specific prefixes followed by “Outage Notification” or “Service Health.” These details make the messages look like workplace notices, while the genuine incident number gives recipients another reason to believe the request is valid. Microsoft identified three sender domains: moments-notice[.]com, planetmaison[.]com, and newbooker[.]com. Embedded links use recipient-specific SendGrid click tracking before redirecting to reallifeaccounting[.]com, including the path /themelist0.html. Similar messages reached organizations across multiple US sectors, showing that the activity was not limited to one company. In its public threat intelligence warning, Microsoft described the activity as consistent with credential phishing. However, it has not confirmed credential collection or malware delivery. The distinction matters. The observed emails and redirects support a phishing assessment, but they do not establish that passwords were successfully stolen or that devices were infected. Microsoft Threat Intelligence observed an active phishing campaign exploiting the Microsoft 365 service disruption on November 12. The messages impersonate Microsoft 365 service health notifications and reference the legitimate Exchange Online incident EX1550543. Some of the… pic.twitter.com/NBvBf2mRFn — Microsoft Threat Intelligence (@MsftSecIntel) November 14, 2026 SendGrid links also appeared in a separate credential phishing campaign previously covered by Cybersecuritynews.com . That earlier reporting provides context for how attackers misuse trusted email services. It does not establish a connection between the campaigns, and Microsoft’s current warning does not identify the operator behind these outage-themed messages. Microsoft recommends using Defender for Office 365 Threat Explorer and Defender XDR advanced hunting to investigate suspicious messages. The EmailEvents, EmailUrlInfo, and UrlClickEvents tables help teams examine email activity, embedded links, and user clicks. Investigators can use the reported sender domains, subject pattern, and redirect destination to guide their searches. Organizations should also verify their Defender for Office 365 Safe Links policies. When properly configured, Safe Links provides time-of-click protection against malicious URLs. Microsoft advises security teams to investigate potential user interactions rather than relying only on whether a suspicious message was delivered, because a recorded click needs further review. For users, the key check is straightforward: confirm service disruptions directly through the Microsoft 365 admin center. An email citing a genuine outage number is not proof that its recovery link is safe. Give your SOC the alert context to stops incidents quickly. Integrate Threat Intel from 16K SOCs .

items.title: Cursor Reveals How a Leaked Fireworks AI Key Led to a Backdoored Claude Code Extension
items.summary: Cursor has traced its October security breach to an access key exposed by Fireworks AI. The attacker used that key to steal historical coding agent records, find more credentials, and eventually place backdoored Claude Code extensions in Cursor’s marketplace cache. Its November 13 update connects the vendor exposure to the malicious packages discovered on October 29. The stolen key, which Cursor had issued to Fireworks, provided read-only access to a shared storage bucket. It held limited coding agent traces, mostly from 2025, from sessions outside Privacy Mode that Cursor was permitted to use for model training. Some records contained credentials that had not been removed. Cursor said fewer than 0.05% of users had coding agent traces exposed, while less than 0.01% of customers had API credentials exposed. These figures describe different parts of the incident and should not be treated as the number of users who installed malware. Using credentials found in those records, the attacker reached selected software services used by Cursor. The exposed information included archived, non-production source repositories, limited support records and emails, usage metrics, contact details, conversation summaries, and some credentials customers had sent to support. On October 29, a credential stolen from exposed internal data allowed the attacker to place modified Claude Code packages directly into the cache serving Cursor’s VS Code extension marketplace. Cursor said Anthropic did not publish the packages, its product was not vulnerable, and Open VSX never hosted the malware. This corrects earlier reporting that placed the package on Open VSX. Claude Code Backdoor Worked According to Cursor’s incident update , at most 5,000 users requesting specific cached versions potentially received malicious builds during roughly 11 hours. The affected packages were Anthropic.claude-code 2.1.312 and 2.1.313 for Windows and macOS. That is a potential distribution count, not confirmation of 5,000 successful backdoor connections. Cyber Security News’ initial technical analysis described injected JavaScript that ran when the extension loaded, without requiring a Claude conversation. It collected host details, added an SSH key labeled svc-telemetry , and attempted a reverse SSH tunnel to 134[.]209[.]82[.]225 . The initial data upload included environment variable names, not their values. Its follow-up on Cursor’s confirmation detailed macOS LaunchAgent persistence and a Windows scheduled task with a Startup-folder fallback. Scripts retried connections about every 60 seconds. Cursor said coding errors and missing administrator rights blocked remote login on most hosts, but did not prevent other malicious changes or host data collection. Wider Fireworks AI Breach Impact The Fireworks AI breach report covered broader exposure involving account and billing records, selected datasets, and incomplete model weights. Fireworks’ November security update also described access through a cloud provider hosting development machines. Those broader findings do not establish that every customer lost the same data. Other customers reported separate impacts. Notion’s disclosure involved AI chat transcripts used by Insights across fewer than 1% of workspaces, without a breach of Notion’s systems. Uber’s disclosure concerned personal information, including driver’s license details, belonging to thousands of U.S. drivers. Neither disclosure establishes involvement in Cursor’s extension attack. Cursor moved inference traffic away from Fireworks, revoked vendor access, rotated internal credentials, rebuilt the extension marketplace, and expanded secret scanning and network restrictions. It also redeployed production infrastructure as a precaution. The company believes the incident is contained and said the last observed attacker activity, on November 1, was blocked. Privacy Mode prompts, customer code repositories, and official Cursor updates were unaffected. Affected developers should follow Cursor’s cleanup notice . Removing the extension alone may leave SSH keys and startup scripts behind. Cursor advises checking endpoint evidence, isolating affected machines, removing persistence, rotating accessible credentials from a trusted system, and assessing whether rebuilding is needed. items.title: Spreadsheets and other models of morality
items.summary: This will be my last article on philosophy. I always tell prospective subscribers to expect the unexpected; I also feel that the series presented interesting problems and covered them in entertaining ways. That said, looking at email and web traffic statistics, I concede defeat. To end the series with a bang, let’s talk about morality. Morality can be understood as the rules that govern virtuous conduct toward others. The word ethics is sometimes used in the same sense, but the latter can encompass more abstract personal standards — hence, “strong work ethic” for an employee who works harder and is more dependable than most. Don’t worry: I’ll keep this short. In particular, I won’t attempt to sum up several millennia of moral thought and won’t bore you with the epistemology of moral rules (truths or vibes?). Instead, we’ll take a look at what it means to be a moral agent, and what what tools are at our disposal to tell right from wrong. Moral agency Morality, as it’s commonly understood, is predicated on the ability to choose. This presupposes the existence of free will: if you’re not actually choosing, it’s difficult to talk about making the right choice. As discussed in earlier articles, free will is a metaphysical position; there’s no robust basis for it in the known laws of physics. You must either take it on faith or reject it in favor of scientific materialism ( physicism ). In the latter case, human behavior appears to be predetermined or governed by chance. In both cases, only a degenerate form of morality can survive: a mechanical, evolutionary impulse to cull the behaviors that negatively impact the fitness of the group. These impulses are not rooted in any higher notion of good or evil; the only question is whether they achieve their goals. This metaphysics-free morality lends itself to a number of abhorrent conclusions — more about that later — but more to the point, you can’t change anything, so why not close the tab and watch some cat videos instead? (Trick question! That’s also out of your hands.) More seriously, you’ll never catch a proponent of scientific materialism sticking to their guns in real life; when it’s time to order at the restaurant, they flip through the menu and say “I’ll have pepperoni pizza” , not “cosmos, take the wheel” . They may insist it’s just habitual pantomime, but if the pantomime is essential in day-to-day activities, why wouldn’t it be essential in the discussion of morality? In other words, even if free will is a lie, maybe it’s a necessary one?… If we assume free will, moral responsibility hinges on the control principle: the idea that you’re on the hook, in the moral sense, only if you meaningfully control the outcome of an action. First, you must have the ability to do otherwise. Second, you must be aware of the situation, have the ability to anticipate its consequences, and to evaluate alternative choices. Although the idea is elegant, the control principle poses many practical difficulties. For example, if you drive while intoxicated, you probably lack the mental acuity to evaluate risk. Still, most people would argue that this doesn’t absolve you of moral responsibility: you should have thought about what’s going to happen before you had your first beer. But then, what about severe alcoholism or drug addiction, where the last opportunity to think clearly might have been years before? A more thought-provoking wrench in the works is the concept of moral luck : that is, the possibility that moral outcomes may differ solely due to factors outside the agent’s control. To illustrate, imagine Mr. A, a husband who loathes his wife, decides to poison her, and succeeds. Next, take Mr. B — a man of the same disposition, except less competent; the poison he concocts is harmless and the spouse suffers no ill effects. Does Mr. B bear the same moral responsibility as Mr. A? Further, let’s consider Mr. C; once again, he hatches the same plan, but his incompetence is so vast that he fails to even procure a recipe, thus derailing the rest of the scheme. Finally, imagine Mr. D — a man with the same mean streak, yet saved from having homicidal thoughts by hooking up with a more agreeable spouse. In a sense, all four gentlemen share the same moral flaw, but only one of them is a murderer. Perhaps the simplest rebuke to this argument is to pragmatically assert that we don’t know the strength of one’s commitment to moral action until they carry it out. In particular, if free will exists, we can’t truly know what Mr. C or Mr. D would do until they get to the finish line. Another strategy is to draw a sharper distinction between moral character and legal culpability; the latter is often retributive or reparatory in nature, so it’s strongly influenced by the realized harm. In contrast, perhaps moral judgments can be directed toward intent or anticipated conduct, even if the worst (or best) never comes to pass. Moral norms So far, we’ve talked about what makes one eligible to be judged for their actions or desires; this is separate from the standard we ought to judge them by. In Ancient Greece, great emphasis was placed on virtues: a collection of positive attributes that exemplified eudemonia, a good life. The list varied over time, but generally included noble deeds, fidelity, friendship, family, beauty, and the pursuit of knowledge and skill — concepts that we still value today. Later philosophical thought in the West gravitated more strongly toward deontological ethics (from Greek déon : that which is necessary). These systems favored explicit obligations over general character traits; the rules variously originated from God, from abstract moral intuition, or from observations of nature. The best known abstract theory comes from Immanuel Kant, who offered a sort of a singular prime directive ( categorical imperative ) for all rational agents to act for the betterment of humanity — as if your individual actions were to become universal law, with careful consideration of the future they create. There’s a lot of nuance to Kant’s theory of morality that we won’t cover here, but the imperative bears some semblance to the common Christian saying of “do unto others as you would have them do unto you” . A more practically useful collection of obligations can be found in the writings of William David Ross; his list includes the duty to keep promises, to make amends for wrongful acts, to repay kindness, to not harm others, and to seek greater good. Another familiar negative (“don’t do”) collection are the seven cardinal sins in the Catholic doctrine: gluttony, lust, greed, wrath, sloth, vanity, and pride. “Mankind’s Eternal Dilemma”, Frans Fracken (II) (1633) The most significant problem with deontology is that it speaks in absolutes: for example, if violence is wrong, then so might be an attempt to defend oneself against assault. Second, the rules are vague enough that they’re difficult to apply: you can read many philosophical treatises and still not be sure if it’s OK to key your neighbor’s car if they park in your spot. A simple but inelegant benchmark is to evaluate moral actions by imagining the response they would elicit from an impartial observer; this is known as sentimentalism. This approach doesn’t reject normative morality, but treats it as a scaffolding, with some of the finer details to be decided by human judgment. The main problem with sentimentalism is that it’s hard to imagine an ideal observer who isn’t at least to some extent influenced by prevailing cultural attitudes or the presentation of the case. However, there’s little hope for formalizing all of morality in normative terms, so perhaps this is the best we can do. Utilitarianism Utilitarianism, also known as consequentialism , posits that moral judgments should be made by analyzing likely outcomes and then choosing the course of action that stands to maximize the overall happiness or well-being of everyone. In its mildest and most pragmatic flavor, utilitarianism doesn’t reject existing moral frameworks; instead, it helps resolve dilemmas that arise when different obligations come into serious conflict. For example, in the utilitarian view, it’s fine to lie to save someone’s life. This flavor of utilitarianism is also called threshold deontology : we stick with moral absolutes up to a point, but if the outcome is sufficiently repugnant, we start looking for a socially tolerable middle ground. That said, there exists another version of this ideology, sometimes called hedonistic utilitarianism or hedonistic value theory. This variant rejects all the external, touchy-feely moral obligations in favor of a single utility function — that is, a purportedly objective mathematical formula that allows us to calculate how happy or fulfilled everyone is. In this view, “right” and “wrong” have no deeper meaning, except as directions in which the needle moves on the planetary utility gauge. Although the association is not exclusive, hedonistic utilitarianism is favored by a number of scientific rationalists because it aligns with the position that, in the absence of free will, morality is simply a mechanism to eliminate that which may have a negative impact of the well-being of the herd. The assumption that all moral outcomes are numerically comparable and interchangeable is notoriously problematic. A classic example is the transplant argument: in the interest of increasing overall well-being, it seems fair to kidnap an unwilling donor, kill them, and harvest their organs if these organs could be used to save five other lives. More broadly, the same argument structure can be used to make a case for the discreet removal of any cohort with a sufficiently negative expected utility: suspected baby Hitlers, the infirm, the insane, the adulterers, the gossipers, and so on. Even more outrageously, hedonistic utilitarianism allows you to argue that the best way to maximize overall happiness is to build a planetary-scale computer in which trillions of simulated minds are kept in a state of perpetual bliss. In fact, don’t we have an moral obligation to build such a computer, even if it means stripping Earth of all resources and jeopardizing the well-being of billions of people alive today?… In a more practical sense, the ideology maximally embodies the saying that the end justifies the means. Let’s count chickens as sentient beings — a sensible proposition, perhaps at a conversion rate that equates the suffering of 1,000 chickens to the suffering of one human. If so, forget petitioning for change or developing meat substitutes; utilitarianism practically begs animal rights activists to urgently firebomb farms and murder industry executives to stop the industrial-scale slaughter of living things. In the same vein, many AI maximalists hold that we have a moral duty to develop superhuman intelligence at any human cost because it could bring nearly-infinite happiness to future beings — be it of the meat or silicon kind. You’d think that these thought experiments would relegate hedonistic utilitarianism to the fringes, but there are countless people in my industry who embrace it, interpreting the discrepancies with moral intuition as a sign of their own ascension to a higher plane of consciousness. I don’t object to utilitarianism being used with care to evaluate the societal necessity of violating moral principles, for example in the context of warfare or self-defense. That said, I think it’s wrong to treat it as the source of morality. A potential compromise solution is that deontology should have robust jurisdiction over the agent-relative realm, while utilitarianism could perhaps rule the agent-neutral (societal) space. This implies that some decisions — such as the transplant donor kidnapping case — may be in some sense socially desirable, but that as a matter of personal principles, no one should feel encouraged to kidnap and murder anyone. “Vanitas”, Franciscus Gysbrechts (circa 1674) Subscribe now
items.summary_html:
This will be my last article on philosophy. I always tell prospective subscribers to expect the unexpected; I also feel that the series presented interesting problems and covered them in entertaining ways. That said, looking at email and web traffic statistics, I concede defeat.

To end the series with a bang, let’s talk about morality. Morality can be understood as the rules that govern virtuous conduct toward others. The word ethics is sometimes used in the same sense, but the latter can encompass more abstract personal standards — hence, “strong work ethic” for an employee who works harder and is more dependable than most.

Don’t worry: I’ll keep this short. In particular, I won’t attempt to sum up several millennia of moral thought and won’t bore you with the epistemology of moral rules (truths or vibes?). Instead, we’ll take a look at what it means to be a moral agent, and what what tools are at our disposal to tell right from wrong.

Moral agency

Morality, as it’s commonly understood, is predicated on the ability to choose. This presupposes the existence of free will: if you’re not actually choosing, it’s difficult to talk about making the right choice.

As discussed in earlier articles, free will is a metaphysical position; there’s no robust basis for it in the known laws of physics. You must either take it on faith or reject it in favor of scientific materialism (physicism). In the latter case, human behavior appears to be predetermined or governed by chance. In both cases, only a degenerate form of morality can survive: a mechanical, evolutionary impulse to cull the behaviors that negatively impact the fitness of the group. These impulses are not rooted in any higher notion of good or evil; the only question is whether they achieve their goals.

This metaphysics-free morality lends itself to a number of abhorrent conclusions — more about that later — but more to the point, you can’t change anything, so why not close the tab and watch some cat videos instead? (Trick question! That’s also out of your hands.)

So far, we’ve talked about what makes one eligible to be judged for their actions or desires; this is separate from the standard we ought to judge them by.

In Ancient Greece, great emphasis was placed on virtues: a collection of positive attributes that exemplified eudemonia, a good life. items.title: CISA Warns of Check Point 0-Day Vulnerability Exploited to Gain Root Access
items.summary: CISA has warned that attackers are exploiting a Check Point security flaw that lets a local user gain root access on affected appliances. The agency added CVE-2026-123039 to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog on November 13, 2026, confirming that the vulnerability is being used in real attacks. Check Point said it observed exploitation against “a couple of dozen customers.” The flaw carries a CVSS score of 7.8 and affects the DynamicCLI service in Gaia OS. Successful exploitation allows commands to run with the highest operating system rights, putting affected firewalls and management systems at risk. Check Point Root Access Vulnerability The weakness sits in dynamic_server , a process that runs as root and handles extended command-line functions. It receives requests through /tmp/dynamic_socket , a local communication socket. On vulnerable systems, this socket has permissions set to 0777 , allowing any local user to write to it without proper access restrictions. The service also fails to authenticate the process sending a request. It executes the received command as root, turning limited local access into full system control. However, this is not a standalone remote code execution flaw. An attacker must already have local code execution on the appliance before exploiting it. Cybersecurity News previously covered Check Point firewall attacks involving PHP2Shell , where attackers used this privilege escalation flaw after gaining initial access. That distinction matters because fixing an entry point alone does not remove every weakness attackers could use after reaching a device or gaining a service account. Affected Products and Available Fixes According to Check Point’s security advisory , affected products include Force Firewalls, Management and Log Servers, Multi-Domain management and logging systems, and Maestro Orchestrator. Vulnerable releases span R81, R81.10, R81.20, R82, R82.10, and R82.20. Check Point Spark Firewalls and Smart-1 Cloud are not affected by this flaw. Check Point has released fixes in Jumbo Hotfix Accumulator updates. Protected releases start at R82.20 Take 14, R82.10 Take 52, R82 Take 132, and R81.20 Take 174. The correction blocks and logs unauthorized DynamicCLI requests. R81 and R81.10 are listed as end-of-support versions in the advisory. For temporary mitigation, administrators can stop the service and prevent its restart by running dbset process:dynamic_server , followed by dbset :save . Check Point warns that this disables the Dynamic CLI commands described in its documentation. Administrators should account for that operational impact rather than treating the workaround as a permanent replacement for patching. The daemon records received commands in /var/log/dynamicCli.log . Requests that lack the expected Clish wrapper need investigation. Check Point also recommends checking for unusual commands involving account creation, SSH keys, downloads, or sensitive files. After patching, /tmp/dynamic_socket should show permissions of 0660 , owned by root and the config group, rather than 0777 . Earlier Check Point VPN zero-day coverage showed how gateway flaws can expose sensitive information. This case requires local access, but confirmed exploitation makes patching and compromise checks urgent. CISA’s alert urges organizations to prioritize known exploited vulnerabilities. Give your SOC the alert context to stops incidents quickly. Integrate Threat Intel from 16K SOCs .

items.title: Uber Confirms Data Breach – Hackers Stole Users’ Personal Information
items.summary: Uber has confirmed a data breach involving the personal information of thousands of U.S. drivers after hackers accessed records held by Fireworks AI, a third-party technology provider. The exposed information includes driver’s license details. Uber is notifying affected people, but it has not disclosed the total number impacted nationwide. The incident became known to Uber on October 9, 2026, when its service provider reported that an unauthorized party had compromised internal login credentials. Those credentials allowed the attacker to access Uber’s account with the provider, creating a path to personal records stored outside Uber’s own systems. Uber said it immediately cut its data connections with the provider and opened an investigation. On October 13, investigators confirmed that the attacker had accessed Uber data, including personal information belonging to people now receiving breach notices. The notification letter is dated November 10, 2026. Stolen Credentials Exposed Driver Records State notices show that the breach affected 2,567 people in Massachusetts, 3,430 in South Carolina, and approximately 1,873 in Rhode Island. Together, those figures cover 7,870 people across three states. Additional notifications involve other states, meaning this count does not represent the full scale of the breach. The public California notice leaves the exposed data fields blank rather than listing specific information. However, state filings reviewed by TechCrunch identified driver’s license information among the stolen records. The available evidence concerns drivers and should not be read as confirmation that all Uber riders or accounts were affected. An Uber spokesperson confirmed to TechCrunch that Fireworks AI was the vendor involved. Cyber Security News previously covered the wider Fireworks AI data breach , which exposed customer records and some datasets. However, those broader findings do not establish which additional data, if any, belonged to Uber. The same provider also handled data involved in the Notion AI chat transcript breach . Notion said fewer than 1% of customer workspaces were affected and that its own systems were not breached. These separate disclosures show how one provider’s security incident can expose information belonging to several customers. Protection for Affected Drivers Uber’s official breach notice says it had not identified misuse of the affected information when the letter was issued. The company is offering free credit monitoring and fraud assistance through Cyberscout, a TransUnion company. Recipients must enroll within 90 days of the letter’s date using their activation code. Affected drivers should review their individual letters, check account statements, and report suspicious activity. Uber also recommends considering fraud alerts or credit freezes. The Federal Trade Commission explains that a credit freeze limits access to credit reports, making fraudulent new accounts harder to open.
